title: Get started — browser & download
combinedTranscript: Learn in your browser first. You do not need to install anything for Module 1 online. Open Start Here and pick Python, C sharp, or A I. Mark steps done as you go — progress stays in this browser. When you want files on your computer, open GitHub’s Code menu. Choose Download ZIP. Find the file in Downloads and unzip it. Git is optional — the ZIP is fine for beginners. Open the right folder for your course. Python is in python-beginner-workbook. C sharp is in csharp-beginner-workbook. Start with each track’s Module 1 setup guide. Quick tip: if a download goes missing, check Help under Downloads. You can keep learning online while tools install. Guest mode works offline after pages load.

title: Python — download, install, first script
combinedTranscript: Install Python from python.org slash downloads. On Windows, tick Add Python to PATH before you install. On Mac or Linux, run the installer or use python 3. Verify it worked. Open Terminal or Command Prompt. Run python dash dash version, or python 3 dash dash version. You should see something like Python 3.11 or newer. Install a code editor such as Cursor or Visual Studio Code. Add the Python extension. Then open your python-beginner-workbook folder. Create hello.py with print Hello. Run python hello.py. Change the message — that is your first real program. If Windows cannot find Python, reinstall and tick Add to PATH. Use the editor’s integrated terminal. Finish Module 1 exercises, then take the quiz.

title: C# — install .NET and first project
combinedTranscript: Install the dot net S D K from dotnet.microsoft.com slash download. Download the latest S D K — version 8 or newer. Run the installer, then finish. Open Terminal or Command Prompt. Run dotnet dash dash version. A number like 8 point 0 means you are ready. Install Cursor or Visual Studio Code. Add the C sharp Dev Kit extension. Open the csharp-beginner-workbook folder in the editor. Create a console app with dotnet new console. Move into the folder with cd. Run dotnet run, then edit Program.cs to make it yours. Remember: C sharp is the language. Dot net is the toolbox. Open the whole project folder, finish Module 1, then take the quiz.

title: Tips & tricks for this site
combinedTranscript: Follow Start Here in order. Open Module 1 online before you install tools. Pick one course and stay with it. Use Mark done so your path updates. Read each lesson, then take the module quiz. Continue banners bring you back where you left off. Certificates unlock when every module is complete. Guest progress stays in this browser. A free account can sync when the cloud is up. Keep guest progress as a backup on free hosting. Type the examples — do not only read them. Break big tasks into tiny checkpoints. When stuck, re-read the tip boxes, then open Help. You are ready. Go to Start Here, choose a course, and open Module 1. Watch the Python or C sharp install video when you code locally.

title: AI Module 1 — foundations lesson
combinedTranscript: Today’s lesson goal: treat A I work as engineering, not magic. You will name what models do well and where they fail. You will leave with a spec and evaluation habit you can reuse. An L L M, or language model, predicts likely next tokens from patterns. It can sound confident even when guessing. Your constraints keep it useful. Strengths you can trust more: drafting and rewriting text you will review. Summarising meeting notes into action lists. Transforming content into a format you define. Watch for failure modes. Hallucinations invent facts or owners. Brittleness means tiny wording changes break output. Injection risk means untrusted text tries to override your rules. Worked example: a support ticket. Goal: a summary and next steps from the ticket. Constraint: only use the provided text. Failure to avoid: inventing a refund promise. Use the engineering loop: spec, prompt, evaluate, iterate. Write the goal, inputs, outputs, and failure modes. Keep a ten-case evaluation set and rerun it after each change. Practice before you finish. Copy the beginner starter pack templates. Write a one-page summariser spec. Build ten evaluation cases for good, bad, and ambiguous inputs. Then continue in the written Module 1 lesson.

title: Python Module 2 — variables & input lesson
combinedTranscript: Today’s lesson goal: store values in variables. Ask the user questions with input. Calculate and display clear results. Variables are labeled boxes. Write customer underscore name equals Sarah. Python picks the type for you. Assign again whenever you want to update the value. Common types you will use: text strings like hello. Whole numbers and decimals like 3 and 9.99. True or False for yes or no decisions later. Worked example: a greeting. Store input Your name in a variable called name. Then print an f-string Hello name. Type it yourself — do not only read it. Worked example: price with tax. Read the price as text. Convert it with float — that turns text into a number. Multiply by one point two for example tax. Print the total with two decimal places. Common mistakes: forgetting float before math on input. Mixing up one equals for assignment with two equals for comparison. Leaving quotes unclosed in strings. Practice, then quiz. Build the greeting and wage calculator exercises. Check solutions only after your own attempt. Take the Module 2 quiz when ready. Then continue in the written lesson.

title: C# Module 2 — variables & input lesson
combinedTranscript: Today’s lesson goal: declare typed variables in C sharp. Read input and convert numbers safely. Calculate totals people can understand. Declare with a type. String customer name equals Sarah. Int quantity equals 3. Double price equals 9.99. The type tells C sharp what kind of box you are creating. Types help beginners. The compiler catches many mistakes early. You see what each value is meant to be. Names plus types document your intent. Worked example: a greeting. Write a prompt. Read the line into a string name. Then write Hello name with string interpolation. Worked example: a tax total. Read a line of text. Parse it with double dot Parse to get a number. Multiply by one point two. Print the total with clear wording. Common mistakes: using the value before Parse succeeds. Forgetting that ReadLine returns text. Opening a single file instead of the whole project folder. Practice, then quiz. Complete the Module 2 exercises in your console app. Compare with solutions after you try. Take the Module 2 quiz. Then continue in the written lesson.

title: AI Module 2 — prompting basics lesson
combinedTranscript: Today’s lesson goal: turn vague asks into clear prompts. Separate role, task, constraints, and format. Test outputs before you trust them. Use a prompt recipe. Role: who the model should act as. Goal: what success looks like. Add constraints and an output shape you can check. Compare vague versus specific. Vague says summarise this meeting. Specific asks for actions, owners, and deadlines as a J S O N list. Specific prompts fail loudly — that is useful. Worked rewrite: add role project assistant. Require only using the notes provided. Return bullets in the shape action, owner, date. Use a few-shot example when it helps. Show one short correct example close to your real format. Remove examples that teach the wrong pattern. Test before you trust. Try good, empty, and conflicting inputs. Score format, factuality, and helpfulness. Tighten the rules, then retest the same cases. Practice checkpoint: rewrite one vague request from your day. Save the before and after in the starter pack. Then continue in the written Prompting Basics lesson.

title: Python Module 3 — decisions & loops lesson
combinedTranscript: Today’s lesson goal: make decisions with if, elif, and else. Compare values and combine conditions. Repeat work with for and while loops. Why control flow matters. Programs choose paths for discounts, menus, and checks. Loops process lists without copy-paste. This is the logic behind everyday apps. Decisions use if, elif, and else. Ask a true or false question. Run one branch when the answer is true. Use elif for more cases, and else for the rest. Worked example: a discount. If spend is over one hundred, apply ten percent. Elif spend is over fifty, apply five percent. Otherwise no discount — print the final total. Loops: use for to walk through a known collection. Use while to keep going until a condition changes. Avoid infinite loops — always update the condition. Common mistakes: using a single equals instead of double equals in comparisons. Forgetting indentation under if or for. While true with no break or stop condition. Practice checkpoint: build a tiny menu or age check. Loop through a short list and print each item. Then continue in the written Module 3 lesson and quiz.

title: Python Module 4 — functions lesson
combinedTranscript: Today’s lesson goal: pack steps into named functions. Pass inputs with parameters. Return results you can reuse. A function is a reusable recipe with a clear name. Call it whenever you need that work done. It keeps programs shorter and easier to test. Parameters are inputs the function receives. Return sends a value back to the caller. Prefer return over only printing when you need the result later. Worked example: define greet with a name parameter. Return a friendly string. Call it with different names. Reuse one function instead of copying print lines. Scope in plain words: names inside a function are local by default. Pass what you need in. Return what you need out. Avoid relying on hidden global variables. Common mistakes: forgetting parentheses when calling. Forgetting return and wondering why you get None. Functions that try to do five unrelated jobs. Practice checkpoint: write one function that calculates a total. Call it twice with different inputs. Then continue in the written Module 4 lesson and quiz.

title: Python Module 5 — collections lesson
combinedTranscript: Today’s lesson goal: store many values in lists. Look up data with dictionaries. Choose the right collection for the job. Lists are ordered collections. Keep items in order and access by index. Append, remove, and loop through items. Great for playlists, baskets, and queues. Dictionaries map a key to a value — like a labelled folder. Use them for fast lookups such as name to email or id to score. Keys must be unique. Worked example: keep a list of friend names and a dictionary of name to phone number. Loop the list and print each number from the dictionary. Common mistakes: off-by-one index errors. Assuming a key exists without checking — use get or check first. Mixing up list order with dictionary keys. Practice checkpoint: build a tiny shopping list or contact book. Add, print, and look up one item. Then continue in the written Module 5 lesson and quiz.

title: Python Module 6 — objects lesson
combinedTranscript: Today’s lesson goal: model real things with classes. Create objects with their own data. Call methods that use that data. A class is the blueprint. An object is one built example. Many objects can share the same class. Attributes store data on the object. Methods are functions tied to the object. Self means this particular object. Worked example: a Task class with a title and done flag. A mark done method flips the flag. Create two tasks and mark one complete. Common mistakes: forgetting self in method definitions. Calling methods incorrectly on the class instead of an instance. Putting all logic in one giant class. Practice checkpoint: create a simple class for a book or student. Add one method and call it. Then continue in the written Module 6 lesson and quiz.

title: Python Module 7 — Task Tracker project lesson
combinedTranscript: Today’s lesson goal: build a small Task Tracker end to end. Combine variables, decisions, loops, and functions. Ship something you can show on a portfolio. Design before you code. List features like add, list, complete, and quit. Decide how tasks are stored. Sketch the menu loop on paper first. Use a core loop pattern. Show a menu. Read the user’s choice. Run the matching action, then show the menu again. Make it robust. Handle empty input and bad menu choices. Confirm before deleting if you add delete. Keep messages clear for beginners testing your app. Common mistakes: building every feature before the menu works. No way to quit the loop. Mixing storage format so list and complete disagree. Practice checkpoint: get add and list working first. Then add complete and quit. Then continue in the written Module 7 project and acceptance checks.

title: C# Module 3 — decisions & loops lesson
combinedTranscript: Today’s lesson goal: use if, else if, and else in C sharp. Compare values safely. Repeat work with for and while. Decisions in C sharp: conditions go in parentheses. Blocks use curly braces. Else if chains handle multiple cases. Worked example: ticket price. Choose child, adult, or senior based on age. Print the matching price. Otherwise ask for a valid age. Loops in C sharp: for when you know the count. While when you wait for a condition. Foreach when you walk a collection. Common mistakes: using a single equals instead of double equals. Missing braces so only one line is conditional. Off-by-one errors in for loops. Practice checkpoint: write a small menu with three options. Loop until the user quits. Then continue in the written Module 3 lesson and quiz.

title: C# Module 4 — methods lesson
combinedTranscript: Today’s lesson goal: write methods that do one clear job. Pass arguments and return values. Keep Main short by calling helpers. Methods are named actions. Declare return type, name, and parameters. Void means it returns nothing. Call methods to reuse logic. Worked example: a Total method that takes price and quantity. Return price times quantity. Print the result from Main. Common mistakes: wrong return type for the value you send back. Forgetting return in non-void methods. Huge methods that mix input, math, and printing. Practice checkpoint: extract one repeated calculation into a method. Call it twice from Main. Then continue in the written Module 4 lesson and quiz.

title: C# Module 5 — collections lesson
combinedTranscript: Today’s lesson goal: use lists for ordered items. Use dictionaries for key lookups. Loop collections with foreach. List stores items in sequence. Dictionary maps keys to values. Pick the structure that matches the problem. Worked example: a list of player names and a dictionary of name to score. Foreach name, print the score. Common mistakes: using arrays when a List is easier to grow. KeyNotFound when a key is missing. Mutating a collection while foreach runs. Practice checkpoint: store three items and print them. Look up one value by key. Then continue in the written Module 5 lesson and quiz.

title: C# Module 6 — objects lesson
combinedTranscript: Today’s lesson goal: create a simple class in C sharp. Add properties and a method. Construct objects and use them. A class defines fields or properties. New creates an instance. Methods act on that instance’s data. Worked example: a Book with Title and IsRead properties. A MarkRead method. Create two books and mark one read. Practice checkpoint: model one real-world thing as a class. Add one behaviour method. Then continue in the written Module 6 lesson and quiz.

title: C# Module 7 — Task Tracker project lesson
combinedTranscript: Today’s lesson goal: assemble a console Task Tracker. Use methods and a list of tasks. Deliver a portfolio-ready mini app. Build in thin slices. Menu loop first. Add and list next. Complete and quit last. Robust behaviour: validate menu choices. Ignore empty task titles. Show friendly messages for bad input. Practice checkpoint: ship a working add and list flow today. Complete the written project checks. Save a short README of how to run it. Then continue in the written lesson.

title: AI Module 3 — prompt patterns lesson
combinedTranscript: Today’s lesson goal: reuse proven prompt patterns. Extract structured fields reliably. Add a review pass that does not invent facts. Checklist pattern: list required fields explicitly. Say what to do when data is missing. Reject guesses that are not in the source. Decompose then verify: break the job into clear steps. Keep drafting separate from checking. Verify structure before you trust content. Worked example: extract name, account, issue, and urgency as J S O N from an email. Only use the email text. A repair pass fixes invalid J S O N without adding new facts. Practice checkpoint: apply two patterns to the same task. Compare which fails less often. Then continue in the written Module 3 lesson.

title: AI Module 4 — evaluation lesson
combinedTranscript: Today’s lesson goal: build a small evaluation set. Score outputs the same way each time. Iterate with evidence, not vibes. Good evaluation uses ten or more cases — good, bad, and ambiguous. Use a fixed rubric for format, accuracy, and safety. Rerun the same set after each prompt change. Worked example cases: empty input should refuse politely. A clear ticket should extract fields. Conflicting dates should ask, not invent. Practice checkpoint: write five eval cases for your prompt. Score a before and after change. Then continue in the written Module 4 lesson.

title: AI Module 5 — safety basics lesson
combinedTranscript: Today’s lesson goal: spot risky prompts and outputs. Add clear refusal and escalation rules. Keep user data out of places it should not go. Practical safety habits: do not paste secrets into prompts. Refuse harmful or disallowed requests. Document what the system must never do. Worked example: a support bot may summarise tickets from provided text. It must not invent refunds or legal advice. It must escalate threats to a human. Practice checkpoint: write a short safety checklist for your use case. Add two refusal test prompts. Then continue in the written Module 5 lesson.

title: AI Module 6 — workflows lesson
combinedTranscript: Today’s lesson goal: chain steps into a simple workflow. Keep humans in the loop where it matters. Log decisions so you can improve later. Workflow thinking: input, transform, check, output. Each step has a clear owner — model or human. Failures should stop or escalate, not silently invent. Worked example: draft a summary. Validate required fields. A human approves before send. Practice checkpoint: draw a three-step workflow for a real task. Mark which steps need a human. Then continue in the written Module 6 lesson.

title: How to study intermediate modules
combinedTranscript: How these intermediate modules work. Each one builds one practical skill. Read the lesson, try the examples, then take the quiz. Keep notes of decisions and tradeoffs. Use a steady study rhythm. Skim goals first. Type along with worked examples. Only then attempt Core and Better exercises. When you get stuck, re-read the common mistakes section. Simplify the input and retry. Open Help or return to the previous module if needed. Next step: open the written lesson for this module. Mark progress as you complete quizzes. Move on when Core exercises pass your own checks.

title: How to study advanced modules
combinedTranscript: Advanced module expectations: assume beginner fundamentals are solid. Focus on design, tradeoffs, and reliability. Treat each module like a professional brief. How to learn effectively: restate the problem in your own words. Compare two approaches before coding. Write down failure modes you must avoid. Evidence of progress: complete the quiz to check understanding. Keep a short change log of what you tried. Link your notes to the module acceptance criteria. Next step: open this module’s written lesson now. Work Core exercises before Beast Mode. Ask for help early on architecture questions.
